title: Pentecost
hookLine: a yearly renewal of openness to the Spirit
tomorrow: Jesus tells his friends to rest. why does it go wrong at once?

cards: A group chat with friends in four countries, and the translate button doing its best. Now a crowded house in Jerusalem, on a feast day. A sound from heaven, “as of a rushing mighty wind,” fills the room.
Something like fire rests on each person there. They pour into the street talking, and visitors from far-off lands each hear them in their own language. Some are amazed.
Some laugh and say they've been drinking. And the whole crowd asks one question: “What meaneth this?”

teach.h: NOT DRUNK: EVERY NATION, ONE FEAST.
teach.b: Peter stands up and answers. Not drunk, he says; it's far too early in the day. Pentecost was already a feast, and the city was full: “Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven.”

This, Peter says, is what the prophet Joel promised: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams.”
All flesh. Daughters as well as sons, old as well as young.
And here's the detail worth telling a friend tonight: nobody had to switch languages. The Spirit didn't make everyone speak one tongue; each person heard in their own.
Some readers hear an answer to Babel, where languages scattered people. Here the languages stay, and people understand anyway. So why keep a one-time morning every year?
In churches that follow the Christian year, Pentecost comes back as a feast of asking again. Jesus says the Father will “give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him.”

teach.h: THE SPIRIT AND THE BRIDE SAY, COME.
teach.b: And near the Bible's last lines, the asking is one word: “And the Spirit and the bride say, Come.” Churches understand the Spirit's gifts differently; some look for tongues and healing, others for a quieter strength.
The asking starts the same way.

how: In churches that keep the Christian year, Pentecost closes the Easter season, often with red and with prayers asking the Holy Spirit to come; Pentecostal and charismatic Christians give special weight to gifts such as speaking in tongues.

o: the night of the last meal Jesus shared with friends
the feast when the Spirit came and each heard their own language
the day Jesus rose from the tomb outside Jerusalem

p: the sound that filled the house
sons and daughters, young and old

s: at Pentecost, everyone began speaking one holy language
each listener heard them in his own language. the languages stayed.
some in the crowd thought the disciples were drunk
others mocked them; Peter answers that it's far too early in the day.
Joel's promise, as Peter quotes it, is for the young men
sons and daughters, young men and old men: all flesh.

games.q: your youth group hosts dinner for families who just arrived from other countries. few share a language. what fits Pentecost?
o: ask everyone to speak English so it's fair to the hosts.
let each family speak its own language, and work to understand.
skip the talking; just serve the food and keep it simple.
games.why: at Pentecost nobody had to switch: each heard in their own language, and they understood anyway.

practice: Rest your hands open on your knees, palms up, the way you'd leave a window open for a breeze. Let each breath come in without pulling at it. If you pray, the one word from Revelation is enough, come, and then leave room.

wordCard.voice: Pentecost. The feast when the Spirit came on a crowded house, and every listener heard in their own language; kept each year as a day to ask again.

orig.note: Greek: Pentecost, the feast's name in Acts 2.

carryVoice: Carry this: come, one word said by the Spirit and by everyone who hears it. Day seventeen-oh-nine, done.
